title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
extended_summary:
This exploratory study examines how K-12 math educators evaluate lesson plans generated by generative AI systems versus human curriculum designers. The paper addresses a practical question in educational AI: whether GenAI-produced lesson plans are perceived as pedagogically comparable to human-authored plans, and which lesson-plan components benefit most from AI assistance.

The intervention/approach compared three sources of lesson plans: a customized prompt-engineered GPT-4 model, a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model trained on lesson-plan data, and human-created lesson plans retrieved from an open-source repository. Twenty experienced K-12 mathematics educators, all with more than 10 years of teaching experience, reviewed paired lesson plans online over several weeks and selected their preferred plan across four dimensions: warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality. Participants also left written comments explaining their choices, which were analyzed thematically alongside the quantitative preference data.

The study found that human-created lesson plans were generally preferred overall, especially for elementary grades and for instructional elements requiring scaffolding, differentiation, student discourse, and structured collaboration. GenAI plans were more competitive in cool-down/lesson-wrap-up sections, and performance tended to improve in higher grade levels, particularly for the fine-tuned LLaMA model in high school contexts. The authors conclude that GenAI is better suited as an assistive planning tool than a replacement for educators, with human expertise still needed for pedagogical nuance and inclusive instruction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used to generate instructional text and lesson plans.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a customized prompt-based GPT-4 model to generate K-12 mathematics lesson plans for comparison with human curriculum designer lesson plans and a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model.

findings.finding_summary: In pairwise educator preference ratings across 529 lesson-plan pairs (16 educators; 2,116 total evaluations), customized GPT-4 was preferred over fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b in 57.7% of comparisons, but was less preferred than human curriculum designer plans overall (human plans preferred 58.7% vs. GPT-4 41.3%). GPT-4 was especially favored for cool-down sections (59.7% over human plans), while human-authored plans were favored for warm-up, main tasks, and overall quality.
findings.measure: Binary educator preference for warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall lesson quality

identified_tools.name: LLaMA
identified_tools.description: Meta large language model used to generate instructional text and lesson plans.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model trained on expert-designed K-12 lesson plans to generate mathematics lesson plans for comparison with customized GPT-4 and human curriculum designer plans.

findings.finding_summary: In pairwise educator preference ratings across 529 lesson-plan pairs, fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b was preferred less often than customized GPT-4 (42.3% vs. 57.7%) and slightly less often than human curriculum designer plans overall (human plans preferred 53.6% vs. LLaMA-2-13b FT 46.4%). LLaMA-2-13b performed comparatively better in cool-down sections (57.9% over human plans) and was particularly competitive at the high-school level, where it was preferred over human-created plans in 59.2% of comparisons.
findings.measure: Binary educator preference for warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall lesson quality

quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods comparative user study with direct educator preferences, but it is not a randomized field trial and reports no causal learning outcome estimates. Evidence quality is therefore moderate-to-lower for inference about instructional effectiveness.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports preference differences rather than effect sizes on student or teacher outcomes, and no impact estimates are provided. The practical signal is mixed: AI was sometimes preferred in cool-downs, but human-authored plans were generally favored overall.
